A sconce is a light fixture that is attached directly to a wall. It is not a floor lamp, not a ceiling light, not a table lamp — it lives on the wall and sticks out from it. Think of it as a bracket or arm that is fixed to the wall, holding a source of light.

A sconce typically has two parts:

  • A back plate — the flat piece that sits flush against the wall and is used to mount the fixture.
  • An arm or bracket — this juts outward from the wall and holds the light at its tip.

Many sconces also have a decorative shade, a glass globe, or an open flame-like design at the end.

Historically, before electricity existed, a sconce held one or more candles. These were extremely common in castles, churches, grand hallways, and mansions — anywhere people needed light on their walls. The back plate was often made of polished metal (like brass or silver) so it could reflect the candlelight and make the room brighter. You can imagine a medieval stone corridor lit by flickering candle sconces on either side.

Today, sconces are electric wall lights. They serve the same purpose — lighting a wall — but they use a light bulb instead of a candle. Modern sconces are everywhere: hotel corridors, bathroom vanities, bedroom walls, staircases, restaurant dining rooms, and theaters.

The word still refers to both types. If you're in an old castle and you see a metal candle holder on the wall, that's a sconce. If you're in a hotel hallway and you see a decorative wall lamp, that's also a sconce.

The wall-mounted position is the defining feature. No other type of light fixture shares this.

Sconces serve both practical and decorative purposes:

  • They provide ambient lighting — soft, diffused light that fills a room without being harsh.
  • They are used for accent lighting — to highlight a painting, a wall, or an architectural feature.
  • They save floor and table space since they don't need a base or stand.
  • They add visual elegance to a room, especially in pairs on either side of a mirror, bed, fireplace, or doorway.

In British university tradition (particularly at Oxford), a sconce refers to a penalty or fine imposed on someone at a formal dinner for saying or doing something that breaks the dining rules. The person who breaks the rule must drink a large tankard of ale — or pay a fine — as punishment. This meaning is quite niche and you are unlikely to encounter it outside of that specific context.

There is also an older, rare meaning of sconce as a small fort or defensive earthwork, but this is essentially archaic and no longer in active use.

• "The innkeeper lit the sconces along the hallway so guests could find their rooms."
  • "She hung a pair of brushed gold sconces on either side of the bathroom mirror."
  • "The stone walls of the dungeon were lined with iron sconces holding smoky torches."
A sconce is a wall-mounted light fixture — historically a candle holder fixed to a wall, and today any decorative or functional electric light that is attached to and protrudes from a wall.
